questions.question: Let T be a full binary tree with 8 leaves. (A full binary tree has every level full.) Suppose two leaves a and b of T are chosen uniformly and independently at random. The expected value of the distance between a and b in T (i.e., the number of edges in the unique path between a and b) is (rounded off to 2 decimal places) ___________ .
questions.explanation:
8 leaves, height 3. Fix leaf a; b is uniform over the 8 leaves (b can equal a):
- same leaf: distance 0 (1 leaf)
- sibling: distance 2 (1 leaf)
- same subtree of height 2: distance 4 (2 leaves)
- other half: distance 6 (4 leaves)

[latex]E=\frac{0+2+2\times4+4\times6}{8}=\frac{34}{8}=4.25[/latex]

Answer: 4.25

questions.question:
Consider a stack data structure into which we can PUSH and POP records. Assume that each record pushed in the stack has a positive integer key and that all keys are distinct.
We wish to augment the stack data structure with an [latex]O(1) [/latex] time MIN operation that returns a pointer to the record with the smallest key present in the stack

1) without deleting the corresponding record, and
2) without increasing the complexities of the standard stack operations.

Which one or more of the following approach(es) can achieve it?

options.A: Keep with every record in the stack, a pointer to the record with the smallest key below it.
options.B: Keep a pointer to the record with the smallest key in the stack.
options.C: Keep an auxiliary array in which the key values of the records in the stack are maintained in sorted order.
options.D: Keep a Min-Heap in which the key values of the records in the stack are maintained.

questions.explanation:
We need [latex]O(1)[/latex] MIN, without slowing down PUSH/POP.

Approach: store, alongside every pushed record, a pointer to whichever record currently holds the smallest key at or below it in the stack (computed once, at push time, by comparing the new key to the previous top's "min so far" pointer). Pushing just does one comparison and one pointer copy ([latex]O(1)[/latex]); popping just removes the top record (its stored min-pointer disappears with it, automatically restoring the correct min for what's now on top) ([latex]O(1)[/latex]); MIN just reads the top record's stored pointer ([latex]O(1)[/latex]). This works and keeps everything [latex]O(1)[/latex].

A single global pointer to the current minimum fails on POP: if you pop exactly the minimum record, you have no way to find the next-smallest without scanning the rest of the stack. A sorted auxiliary array would need [latex]O(n)[/latex] shifting on push to keep it sorted. A min-heap would make push/pop cost [latex]O(\log n)[/latex] instead of [latex]O(1)[/latex], violating the "don't slow down the standard operations" requirement.

Answer: Keep, with every record, a pointer to the record with the smallest key below it.
